facts.fact: 15-year-old male presented to the ED with a 3-day history of severe lower abdominal pain and constipation.
Initial ED impression was constipation, later associated with mild dehydration.
Abdominal X-ray showed significant faecal loading with no evidence of obstruction or perforation.
Blood tests including FBC, U&Es, CRP, and LFTs were normal.
The patient was treated with IV 0.9% sodium chloride for mild dehydration.
A single 10 mg oral dose of bisacodyl was administered in the ED to initiate bowel movement.
Oral macrogol/Movicol was started for constipation during admission and later discontinued once symptoms resolved.
The patient was referred and admitted to paediatrics for supportive management and observation.
Physiotherapy was provided to encourage gentle mobilisation to improve bowel motility, and the patient tolerated sessions well.
The patient improved clinically with reduction in abdominal pain, passage of a partial bowel movement overnight, then a full bowel movement, and resolution of abdominal pain.
The patient was discharged home after symptom resolution with advice on high-fibre diet and oral hydration.
He was discharged with take-home lactulose 10 mL twice daily as needed for maintenance and recurrence prevention.
The patient presented after a minor fall with acute confusion and disorientation, with an initial GCS of 12/15 that later improved during admission.
CT head showed a subdural hygroma without midline shift or acute intracranial haemorrhage.
FBC, U&E, and coagulation studies were normal initially.
Mild hyponatremia was identified during admission with serum sodium 132 mmol/L and was considered a contributor to confusion.
The patient was admitted to the neurology ward for monitoring and neuro observations, with a repeat CT head planned.
Hyponatremia was treated with oral sodium chloride tablets 1 g three times daily.
Headache after the fall was treated with paracetamol 1 g four times daily by mouth.
Repeat CT head on 03/01/26 showed no progression of the subdural hygroma.
The patient received physiotherapy for gait instability and balance impairment, with gradual improvement over the hospital stay.

Occupational therapy addressed fine motor difficulty and home safety, including recommendations for a raised toilet seat, grab rails, removal of loose rugs, improved lighting, and stair/bathroom handrails.
Speech and language assessment found an adequate swallow and no aspiration, with mild word-finding difficulty thought to be related to residual confusion.
The patient's cognition and mobility improved during admission, and by the end of physiotherapy he was walking independently with a steady gait and GCS 15/15.
The patient was discharged home with community support services and follow-up arranged in neurology outpatient clinic.
Short courses of levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily for 7 days and atorvastatin 40 mg daily for 7 days were started near discharge.
The patient had end-stage osteoarthritis of the left hip causing severe chronic pain and functional limitation, and underwent elective total left hip replacement.
The patient had a history of hypertension, with peri-operative blood pressures mildly elevated but without acute hypertensive complications.
Pre-operative assessment showed mild anaemia with hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL, and ferrous sulfate was started for optimization before surgery.
Pre-operative ECG showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes.
Written informed consent was obtained for the total left hip replacement after discussion of risks, benefits, and recovery expectations.
The patient underwent a total left hip replacement of the left hip under spinal anaesthesia via a posterolateral approach.
Intraoperative findings were severe degenerative changes with significant cartilage loss and no evidence of infection or abnormal surrounding tissue.
The removed left femoral head was sent for histological examination.
A cemented prosthetic implant was placed in the left hip.
Estimated intraoperative blood loss was approximately 150 mL and there were no intraoperative complications.
Immediate postoperative course was stable in PACU, with the patient alert, comfortable, and the surgical site clean and dry; she was transferred to the orthopaedic ward.
Postoperative thromboprophylaxis with enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily was started.
Postoperative pain was managed with paracetamol, including regular dosing initially and PRN use later in the admission.
Postoperative anaemia developed after surgery, with hemoglobin around 104–105 g/L and no acute intervention required initially.
Ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily was prescribed for postoperative anaemia, alongside advice for a high-iron diet and monitoring of hemoglobin.
The patient progressed through physiotherapy from walker-assisted mobilization to crutches, then was deemed safe for independent discharge with crutches.
Occupational therapy provided a hip kit and recommended minor home adaptations, including a raised toilet seat and bathroom grab bars, to support safe activities of daily living.
The postoperative wound remained clean and dry without signs of infection, erythema, discharge, swelling, or DVT signs during ward reviews.
The patient was discharged home on 06/01/26 with follow-up physiotherapy and outpatient clinic arrangements in place.
Discharge medications included rivaroxaban 10 mg once daily for 7 days for postoperative thromboprophylaxis and paracetamol as needed for pain.
The patient had end-stage osteoarthritis of the left hip with severe chronic pain and functional limitation, and was scheduled for elective total left hip replacement.
Pre-operative assessment showed mild anaemia with haemoglobin around 10.8 g/dL, while renal and liver function tests were otherwise normal.
Relevant past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and mild osteopenia.

Pre-operative management included stopping ibuprofen 48 hours before surgery, starting ferrous sulfate for mild anaemia, and starting omeprazole to reduce gastrointestinal side effects from ibuprofen.
The patient underwent elective total left hip replacement under general anaesthesia with spinal block.
Intraoperative findings confirmed severe cartilage erosion and subchondral bone exposure in the left hip without evidence of acute inflammation or infection.
A cemented total hip prosthesis with polyethylene acetabular component and metal femoral component was implanted.
Estimated blood loss during surgery was 300 mL and there were no operative complications.

Immediate post-operative care included enoxaparin for VTE prophylaxis, cefuroxime for infection prophylaxis, and multimodal analgesia with paracetamol and tramadol, with IV morphine used for early post-op pain.
The post-operative course was uncomplicated, with stable vital signs, no bleeding, no nausea or vomiting, and no neurovascular deficits.
Post-operatively, haemoglobin remained mildly low at 10.8 g/dL and ferrous sulfate was prescribed for 4 weeks.

The patient mobilised progressively after surgery with physiotherapy, advancing from early assisted steps to walker use, then crutches, and by discharge could ambulate independently and climb stairs safely.

Occupational therapy identified the need for home adaptations, including a raised toilet seat, bathroom grab rails, and a long-handled reacher, and the patient was eventually cleared for independent activities of daily living.

The patient was discharged home after satisfactory recovery with apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily for 2 weeks, a home exercise programme, and follow-up with the GP in 6 weeks for wound review and outpatient physiotherapy referral.
A 3-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with poor feeding, reduced oral intake, and mild lethargy, with fewer wet nappies suggesting dehydration.
Initial assessment showed mild fever and mild tachycardia, with no respiratory distress and no severe dehydration.
The working diagnosis in the ED was a viral illness / viral upper respiratory tract infection with associated poor feeding and mild dehydration.
The child had allergies to pollen and macrolides.
Paracetamol was given for fever, and oral normal saline fluid bolus / oral rehydration measures were started for dehydration.
He was admitted to the Paediatric Assessment Unit for observation and supportive care, including IV maintenance fluids.
No blood or urine tests were initially performed in the ED.
Subsequent blood gas showed mild metabolic acidosis with venous pH 7.33 and bicarbonate 17 mmol/L.
During admission, hydration and oral intake gradually improved and fever settled, with no respiratory distress.
Nasal congestion persisted during the ward stay and was felt to be part of a viral URTI affecting feeding.
ENT review found moderate nasal mucosal inflammation consistent with viral URTI, without purulent discharge or anatomical abnormality.
Supportive treatment included IV fluids, paracetamol as needed, nasal saline drops, advice on oral rehydration, and later saline spray / steam inhalation for congestion.
He improved enough to be discharged home, with stable observations, no dehydration, and parents educated on home hydration and warning signs.
The patient presented to the ED with acute confusion after a minor fall, initially with GCS 14/15 and mild disorientation.
CT head showed a subdural hygroma with no midline shift and no acute intracranial bleed.
The confusion was attributed to the subdural hygroma, with mild hyponatremia and dehydration felt to be contributing factors.
Neurological examinations remained without focal deficits, with only transient disorientation and mild gait instability/unsteadiness during admission.
Initial laboratory testing was largely normal except for mild hyponatremia, with serum sodium around 132 mmol/L that later improved to 133 mmol/L but remained slightly low.

The patient was treated with intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride for dehydration and hyponatremia, then oral sodium chloride supplementation and fluid restriction were used to manage persistent hyponatremia.
The patient received prophylactic ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily for 5 days during the admission.
Physiotherapy was required for post-fall mobility and balance impairment, with gradual improvement over the admission using walking aids and gait/balance training.

Occupational therapy addressed impaired fine motor/ADL performance and cognitive difficulties, and recommended adaptive equipment such as a button hook, long-handled reacher, non-slip mat, and shower chair.
By discharge, the patient was neurologically stable, oriented, and mobilizing safely with a walking stick, with no headache, dizziness, or confusion.
The patient was discharged home with community care and outpatient follow-up plans, including neurology follow-up in 2 weeks, GP review, and ongoing physiotherapy.
Patient presented with acute confusion after a minor fall/head injury with no reported loss of consciousness.
CT head showed a subdural hygroma without acute intracranial hemorrhage or mass effect.
The acute confusion was managed conservatively with observation and neurological monitoring rather than surgery.
The patient had a documented history of hypertension, osteoarthritis, and a prior TIA in 2018.
Initial neurological status was mildly abnormal with GCS 14/15 and disorientation/confusion but no focal neurological deficits.
The patient had a mild right-sided headache after the fall, treated symptomatically with paracetamol.
Mild dehydration and mild hyponatremia were identified during admission, with serum sodium as low as 131 mmol/L.
Hyponatremia/dehydration were treated with IV normal saline initially and later oral hydration plus electrolyte supplementation, including Dioralyte and sodium chloride tablets.
Serial reviews showed progressive improvement in cognition, with resolution of confusion by discharge.
Serial reviews showed improvement in serum sodium to 133 mmol/L prior to discharge.
Occupational therapy and speech-language therapy identified mild cognitive/word-finding and short-term memory issues early in admission, with recommendation for cognitive rehabilitation exercises.
Physiotherapy documented improving mobility and balance over the admission, progressing to safe independent ambulation and stair assessment prior to discharge.
A home safety assessment identified bathroom and stair hazards, leading to installation of grab rails before discharge.
The patient was discharged home medically fit with community physiotherapy follow-up and GP review arranged.
The patient had end-stage osteoarthritis of the right shoulder causing severe pain, stiffness, reduced range of motion, crepitus, and night pain before surgery.
Pre-operative blood work showed mild anaemia with haemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, and ferrous sulfate was started to optimise haemoglobin before surgery.
Pre-operative ECG and chest X-ray were normal, and other routine blood tests were within acceptable limits.
The patient underwent an elective total right shoulder replacement under general anaesthesia using an anterior deltopectoral approach with layered closure and a cemented modular shoulder prosthesis.
Intra-operative findings showed severe glenohumeral joint degeneration with significant cartilage loss and no evidence of infection or periarticular inflammation.
The operation had minimal blood loss and no intra-operative complications.
Post-operatively, the patient received IV cefuroxime for 24 hours, morphine PCA and other analgesia, shoulder sling immobilisation, wound care, and physiotherapy.
Immediately after surgery in recovery, the patient was stable, awake, had no wound bleeding or haematoma, and was transferred back to the ward.
Post-operative nausea occurred in recovery and was treated with ondansetron.
During the ward stay, the wound remained clean, dry, and without infection, swelling, erythema, discharge, or neurovascular compromise.
Post-operative pain was manageable with analgesia and shoulder mobility improved progressively with physiotherapy.
Enoxaparin was started for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis during the hospital stay.

The patient received physiotherapy education and home exercise programme instruction for shoulder rehabilitation, including sling use, passive and active-assisted range-of-motion exercises, strengthening, and activities of daily living management.
The patient was planned for discharge the day after the final ward review if no new issues arose, with oral paracetamol and follow-up physiotherapy/home exercises.
Pre-operative assessment found the patient fit for general anaesthesia, with hypertension and acid reflux as past medical history and no known drug allergies.
The patient had documented informed consent for the shoulder replacement after discussion of risks, benefits, and recovery/physiotherapy expectations.
The patient is a 4-year-old boy with a history of right tibial fracture treated with internal fixation in 2024.
He has mild asthma, managed with inhalers, and this was considered stable pre-operatively.
He has eczema.
He has documented allergies to penicillin, sulfonamides, pollen, and nuts.
He underwent elective removal of internal fixation hardware from the right tibia under general anaesthesia.
Pre-operative asthma optimisation included montelukast 4 mg once daily for two weeks and pre-operative salbutamol inhaler use.
Pre-operative blood tests (FBC and coagulation screen) were reviewed and were satisfactory for surgery.
At pre-operative assessment, mild wheeze was noted but there was no acute asthma exacerbation or respiratory distress, and the patient was deemed fit for surgery.
Peri-operative antibiotic prophylaxis was planned and given with cefuroxime, with allergy-aware alternative coverage considered.
Intra-operatively, the internal fixation device was removed successfully; the surrounding tissue was healthy, blood loss was minimal, and there were no complications.
Post-operative recovery was uncomplicated: he was fully awake quickly, had stable oxygenation and no nausea, and the wound dressing was intact without bleeding or discharge.
Post-operative course included pain control with paracetamol and a single oral ibuprofen dose in recovery, with pain later well controlled.
Post-operative review noted a clean, healing surgical site without infection, swelling, erythema, or tenderness.
A mildly elevated CRP of 12 mg/L was interpreted as post-operative inflammation, with monitoring planned.
He received post-operative physiotherapy and occupational therapy for mobilisation, gait support, and home exercise/crutch training.
He was discharged the day after surgery with follow-up planned in 2 weeks for wound/suture review, and home instructions for wound care, infection monitoring, pain control, and exercises.
Discharge antibiotics included a 5-day course of cefuroxime suspension, despite the recorded penicillin and sulfonamide allergies.
The patient was diagnosed with reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) after presenting with a sudden severe thunderclap headache triggered by exertion.
She was triaged as Category 2 urgent for the severe exertional headache, with elevated blood pressure around 160/90 mmHg and heart rate around 88 bpm.
Initial neurological examinations were normal, with no focal deficits or signs of raised intracranial pressure.
CT head showed no intracranial haemorrhage or mass lesion.
Blood tests during admission showed mild inflammatory marker elevation and mild leukocytosis with otherwise normal renal and liver function tests.
MRI/MRA of the brain and cerebral vasculature confirmed RCVS and later repeat MRA showed improvement/resolution of vasoconstriction.
She was treated with oral nimodipine during admission for vasospasm/RCVS.
Her headache improved progressively during admission and resolved by discharge, with no new neurological symptoms.
Admission was accompanied by mild hypokalaemia, which was treated with oral potassium supplementation.
She developed mild hyponatraemia during admission, managed with dietary sodium increase and fluid restriction.
She was discharged home after clinical improvement and documented resolution/improvement of vasoconstriction on repeat MRA.
Discharge plan included tapering nimodipine over 2 weeks and neurology outpatient follow-up in 4 weeks.
The patient was diagnosed in the ED with spontaneous pneumomediastinum after presenting with sudden severe central chest pain worsened by deep breathing and movement.
Chest X-ray showed pneumomediastinum with subcutaneous emphysema, and there was no pneumothorax reported.
ECG showed sinus tachycardia without ischaemic changes.
The spontaneous pneumomediastinum was managed conservatively with observation and analgesia, including paracetamol and ibuprofen.
The patient was advised to avoid straining, Valsalva manoeuvres, and heavy lifting because these could worsen the pneumomediastinum.
The patient remained hemodynamically stable throughout admission and had no evidence of respiratory compromise.
Repeat chest imaging showed gradual improvement with slight reduction in the pneumomediastinum, followed by complete resolution on the final CXR.
Analgesics were stopped once the patient became pain-free.
Discharge planning was initiated with outpatient respiratory follow-up arranged and the patient educated about recurrence symptoms and when to seek urgent care.
The patient had end-stage osteoarthritis of the right knee and underwent an elective total right knee replacement.
Pre-operative assessment documented chronic right knee pain with reduced range of motion, intermittent swelling, and occasional night pain despite analgesia.
Relevant past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and prior appendectomy in 1998.
There were no known drug allergies.
Pre-operative ECG showed sinus rhythm without acute abnormalities.
Pre-operative blood tests including FBC, U&Es/renal function, and clotting profile were within acceptable range for surgery.
Hypertension was optimised pre-operatively with amlodipine 5 mg daily.
The patient received informed consent for the operation before surgery.
The operation was performed under general anaesthesia with a cemented total knee prosthesis implanted and absorbable sutures used for closure.
Intra-operative findings were significant cartilage erosion and osteophyte formation consistent with end-stage osteoarthritis.
There were no operative complications and estimated blood loss was minimal.
Immediate post-operative recovery in PACU was stable; pain and mild nausea were treated with morphine and ondansetron, and the patient was cleared for transfer to the orthopaedic ward.
Post-operative analgesia included morphine via PCA, regular paracetamol, and ibuprofen initially, with later adjustment of anti-inflammatory therapy during recovery.
Post-operative thromboprophylaxis was started with enoxaparin and later dalteparin, and at discharge apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily for 14 days was prescribed.
Post-operative antibiotic prophylaxis with cefuroxime 1.5 g IV for 24 hours was given.
Post-operative haemoglobin decreased to 110 g/L without need for transfusion.
Post-operative inflammation was reflected by CRP 45 mg/L, later 44 mg/L, with no evidence of infection.
Recovery progressed with physiotherapy, including improvement in knee flexion to 90 degrees, transition from walker to crutches, and ability to mobilise safely.
The surgical wound remained clean and healing well throughout recovery, with only mild expected swelling and bruising and no signs of infection or DVT.
Occupational therapy recommended crutches and a raised toilet seat to support safe discharge.
Discharge was deemed safe from a physiotherapy standpoint after the patient demonstrated safe stair climbing and mobility with crutches.
The patient presented with sudden severe central chest pain and was diagnosed with spontaneous pneumomediastinum.
Mild subcutaneous emphysema was detected on examination during the initial assessment and early ward course.
Chest X-ray confirmed pneumomediastinum and showed no pneumothorax or other major abnormality.
CT chest confirmed spontaneous pneumomediastinum and showed no oesophageal or tracheal rupture.
The patient was admitted to the Acute Respiratory Ward for conservative management and monitoring.
Management was supportive, including analgesia with paracetamol and ibuprofen, later tapered to PRN use as symptoms improved.
Breathing exercises and physiotherapy were used repeatedly during admission to aid recovery, improve lung expansion, and support mobilisation.
Serial chest radiographs showed progressive improvement, with mild reduction in mediastinal air on 08/01/26 and near-complete resolution by 10/01/26.
The patient's symptoms improved steadily during admission, progressing from severe chest pain to no chest pain and comfortable breathing without respiratory distress.
No complications were identified during the admission, and there was no evidence of oesophageal or tracheal injury.
The patient was discharged with conservative management instructions, breathing exercises, and follow-up chest X-ray planned in 2 weeks.
Discharge medications included ibuprofen and paracetamol as needed for residual discomfort, with salbutamol also provided at discharge.
The patient had end-stage osteoarthritis of the left hip causing chronic pain and reduced mobility, and was admitted for elective total left hip replacement.
Pre-operative evaluation showed mild vitamin D deficiency with a serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of 18 ng/mL.
Pre-operative ECG showed borderline first-degree AV block, which was assessed as not clinically significant.
Relevant comorbidities included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and osteoporosis.
The patient had a penicillin allergy, and clindamycin 600 mg IV was planned/used as peri-operative antibiotic prophylaxis.
The patient underwent elective total left hip replacement under general anaesthesia with cemented total hip prosthesis implantation and removal of the left femoral head.
Intra-operative findings were severe cartilage loss of the femoral head and acetabulum without surrounding inflammation or infection.
The operation had estimated blood loss of 200 mL and no intra-operative complications.
Post-operatively, the patient had expected anaemia with haemoglobin around 10.2 g/dL (110 g/L) after surgery.
Post-operative pain required regular paracetamol and later tramadol 50 mg as needed for breakthrough pain.
VTE prophylaxis was given with enoxaparin initially and then dalteparin 5000 units subcutaneously daily, with discharge prophylaxis planned for 4 weeks.
The post-operative wound remained clean and dry without infection or dehiscence, with only mild bruising/swelling consistent with expected recovery.
The patient progressed with physiotherapy from bed-edge exercises to assisted mobilization and partial weight-bearing with a walker, with improving confidence and stability.
Occupational therapy found that transfers and toilet use required moderate assistance and recommended discharge with mobility aids including a raised toilet seat, long-handled reacher, and walker.

There were no operative or immediate post-operative complications.

Abdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged, non-compressible appendix with peri-appendiceal fluid, consistent with acute appendicitis.
The working diagnosis was acute appendicitis and the patient was admitted under General Surgery/Surgical Assessment Unit.
Pre-operative management included NBM status, IV cefuroxime, IV metronidazole, and IV fluids while awaiting surgery.
The patient underwent laparoscopic appendectomy under general anaesthesia on 01/01/26.
Intra-operative findings were an inflamed appendix without perforation or abscess, and the appendix was removed.
The operation had minimal blood loss and no intra-operative complications.
Post-operatively, the patient recovered well, became alert and stable, and had no nausea, vomiting, or wound complications immediately after surgery.
Post-operative labs and ward review showed improvement, with CRP trending down to 18 mg/L and normal WBC, and there were no signs of infection.
The patient required physiotherapy and occupational therapy during recovery to support mobilization, stairs, and activities of daily living, and progressed to independent mobility.
The patient was treated with analgesia and oral antibiotics during recovery, including paracetamol, ibuprofen, and co-amoxiclav.
The surgical wound remained clean, dry, and healing well throughout the post-operative course without infection or dehiscence.
The patient was discharged after an uncomplicated recovery from laparoscopic appendectomy with advice for light activity and avoidance of heavy lifting for six weeks.

The patient had end-stage osteoarthritis of the left knee causing severe pain and functional limitation, and was admitted electively for total left knee replacement.
Pre-operative assessment identified mild anaemia with hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL, while other blood tests, urinalysis, and ECG were normal.
The patient was started on ferrous sulfate to address mild anaemia before surgery and it was continued peri-operatively/post-operatively.
The patient underwent elective total left knee replacement under general anaesthesia.

Post-operatively, the patient received thromboprophylaxis with tinzaparin initially and later enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily.

The patient has a background of asthma, hypertension, and hypercholesterolaemia.
She presented with 3 days of progressive shortness of breath and increased use of salbutamol without significant relief.
On presentation she was hypoxic, with oxygen saturation 88% on room air, requiring supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula.
Chest X-ray showed right lower lobe consolidation consistent with a lower respiratory tract infection.
Initial blood tests showed inflammatory markers and leukocytosis, including elevated CRP and WCC, with blood cultures sent and pending.
Arterial blood gas showed hypoxaemia, and later clerking documented mild respiratory acidosis.
She was diagnosed with lower respiratory tract infection with right lower lobe consolidation, complicated by hypoxia.
An acute asthma exacerbation was also considered during the admission.
She was admitted under the respiratory team for inpatient management.
Treatment included intravenous co-amoxiclav, later with added intravenous clarithromycin, along with nebulised salbutamol as needed and supplemental oxygen.
Respiratory physiotherapy was provided during admission, focusing on breathing exercises, active cycle of breathing techniques, sputum clearance, mobility, and exercise tolerance.
A dietitian noted mild weight loss and recommended oral nutritional supplements (Fortisip) twice daily.
Her clinical and inflammatory markers improved over the admission, with falling CRP, improved oxygenation, and reduced work of breathing.
She was successfully weaned off supplemental oxygen and maintained oxygen saturation on room air before discharge.
She was discharged with oral amoxicillin/co-amoxiclav to complete the antibiotic course and advised to continue salbutamol and breathing exercises.
Follow-up with primary care or respiratory clinic was arranged after discharge, and she was advised to return if shortness of breath or fever developed.
The patient presented with sudden severe central chest pain radiating to the back, associated with shortness of breath and worse on deep inspiration.
Initial assessment showed tachypnoea and mild hypoxia on room air, with oxygen saturations around 93% and respiratory rate 26-28 breaths/min.
Chest X-ray demonstrated mediastinal air consistent with spontaneous pneumomediastinum, with no pneumothorax.
Arterial blood gas showed mild respiratory alkalosis without significant hypercapnia or acidosis.
Inflammatory markers were not significantly elevated, with CRP normal/2 mg/L and white cell count reported at 12.5 x10^9/L.
The patient was diagnosed with spontaneous pneumomediastinum, considered likely benign with no obvious precipitant.
He was managed conservatively on the acute medical unit with oxygen at 2 L/min via nasal cannula and analgesia including paracetamol, with ibuprofen added as needed.
